children.html: At this point, we have used all six variables, but have one more to make before we reach n - r. Note that the two \Pi variables are disconnected from each other. This is a clear sign that we have an independent quantity/product to construct (that can’t be made from the two). We would like to relate the gravitational piece to R_{\oplus}. The easiest way to do this is \Pi_3 = \frac{R_{\oplus}}{a}. I was tempted to use physical intuition and make \Pi_3 almost identical to \Pi_2 except with (a + R_{\oplus}) in place of a in the denominator—the rationale being that we expect the tidal phenomenon to relate to differential pull across the Earth’s extent. But this is inconsistent with the formal prescription of products, as in Eq. 3. (It still works out fine with this choice, FWIW, and even provides a factor of two getting closer to the truth.) So we end up with:

So we certainly got into the right ballpark. Had we “violated” the rule of strictly product-based <math>\Pi</math> variable construction and used our <math>\frac{GM_m}{g\,(a + R_{\oplus})^2}</math> variable, we would have ended up a bit happier with <math>\frac{2}{3}\,m</math>.
